title: Replication
tagline: Keep copies of your data on multiple machines for read scale, availability, and durability — and manage the lag.
summary: Leader-follower, sync vs async, multi-leader, replication lag.

items.detail: Serve reads from many copies, multiplying read throughput (great for read-heavy systems).
If one node dies, another copy keeps serving — no data loss, minimal downtime.
Data survives a single disk/machine failure because copies exist elsewhere.
Place replicas near users in different regions to cut read latency.

blocks.text: Replication = copies of the *same* data on multiple nodes (for redundancy/read scale). Partitioning/sharding = splitting *different* data across nodes (for write/storage scale). Big systems do both: shard the data, then replicate each shard.

paragraphs: The most common model: one **leader** (primary) accepts all writes; it streams its changes to one or more **followers** (replicas) that serve reads. Clients write to the leader and read from any replica. This scales reads and provides failover — if the leader dies, a follower is promoted.

blocks.caption: Writes go to the leader; the leader replicates to followers; reads spread across followers.

rows: After replica(s) confirm they have it
Risk of losing the last writes
Blocks if a replica is slow/down
Often 'semi-sync': wait for 1 replica, rest async
Default for performance; accept tiny loss window

blocks.text: Pure synchronous (wait for all) is safe but fragile — one slow replica stalls writes. Pure async is fast but can lose recent writes on failover. The common compromise is semi-synchronous: acknowledge once at least one replica confirms, replicate to the rest asynchronously.

paragraphs: With async replication, followers are slightly behind the leader. A user who writes to the leader and immediately reads from a lagging follower may see *old* data — the 'I posted but it's not there' bug. This is replication lag, and it's the practical face of eventual consistency.

items.detail: Route a user's reads to the leader (or a known-caught-up replica) for a short window after they write.
Pin a user to one replica so they don't see time go backwards by bouncing between replicas at different lag.

items.term: Read from leader for critical data
items.detail: For data that must be fresh, just read the leader.

blocks.title: Multi-leader & leaderless (mention if pushed)
blocks.text: Multi-leader: several leaders accept writes (e.g., one per region) and sync to each other — great for multi-region write latency, but you must resolve write conflicts. Leaderless (Dynamo-style, e.g., Cassandra): any replica takes reads/writes, using quorums (W + R > N) and read-repair to stay consistent. These are senior-level talking points.

cheatsheet: Replication = copies of the same data on multiple nodes → read scale, availability, durability, geo-locality.
Leader–follower: one primary takes writes and streams to read replicas; promote a follower on failure.
Sync replication = no data loss but slower/blocking; async = fast but can lose recent writes; semi-sync is the common middle.
Async causes replication lag → stale reads; fix with read-your-writes, monotonic reads, or read-from-leader for critical data.
Multi-leader (per-region writes, needs conflict resolution) and leaderless/quorum (Dynamo/Cassandra, W+R>N) are advanced options.
Replication ≠ sharding: replicate copies, shard splits data. Big systems shard then replicate each shard.

questions.prompt: Your app uses async leader-follower replication. A user changes their profile photo, the write succeeds, but on the next page load they still see the old photo. Explain and fix.
questions.hint: Where did the write go, and where did the read come from?
answer: The write went to the leader, but the follow-up read was served by a follower that hadn't yet received the replicated change (replication lag). So the user sees stale data — a read-your-writes violation caused by async replication.

Fix it narrowly: for a short window after a user writes, route *that user's* reads to the leader (or a replica confirmed to be caught up past their write position), or read the just-written value from a write-through cache. Everyone else can keep reading from followers cheaply. This preserves the read-scaling benefit while guaranteeing each user sees their own updates.
keyPoints: Route own reads to leader/caught-up replica briefly
Keep others on followers (don't make everything synchronous)
followUps: How would you know a replica is 'caught up' past a user's write?

questions.prompt: For a banking ledger, would you use synchronous or asynchronous replication for the primary, and why?
questions.hint: What's the cost of losing the last few acknowledged writes?
answer: Lean synchronous (at least semi-synchronous) for the ledger. If the leader fails right after acknowledging a write, async replication could lose that write — for money, silently losing an acknowledged transaction is unacceptable. Synchronous replication ensures at least one replica has the write before it's acked, so a promoted replica won't lose committed transactions (no data loss / RPO ≈ 0).

The cost is higher write latency and reduced availability if replicas are slow/unreachable — but for a ledger, correctness and durability outweigh latency. A practical setup: semi-sync (ack after one replica in another availability zone confirms), keeping the rest async for read scaling. State the trade-off explicitly: you're choosing durability/consistency over write latency for this specific data.
keyPoints: Sync/semi-sync for money: no loss of acked writes (RPO≈0)
Async risks losing recent committed transactions on failover
Accept higher write latency / lower availability for correctness
Semi-sync (one AZ replica) balances safety and read scale
followUps: How does this choice interact with CAP during a partition between leader and replica?
